passages.title: David laments Saul and Jonathan
passages.summary: An Amalekite brings Saul’s royal objects and claims to have killed him. David orders his death, then laments Saul and Jonathan. The messenger’s claim differs from 1 Samuel 31. The guide preserves that difference instead of treating both accounts as identical.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual treats the messenger’s claim as deception. This remains its interpretation of the differing accounts.

passages.title: Two kingdoms and the battle at Gibeon
passages.summary: Judah anoints David at Hebron. Abner installs Ishbosheth at Mahanaim. Fighting at Gibeon leads to Asahel’s death. A contest expands into broader killing. The division and pursuit reveal the human costs of succession.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: examine how competition becomes violence and what stopping it requires.

passages.title: Abner changes allegiance and Joab kills him
passages.summary: After conflict with Ishbosheth over Rizpah, Abner negotiates with David. Michal is returned. Joab kills Abner, and David mourns. Women’s household positions enter negotiations over power. David publicly rejects responsibility for Abner’s killing.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: consider people’s interests when leaders negotiate control over their households.

passages.title: Ishbosheth is murdered
passages.summary: Rechab and Baanah kill Ishbosheth and bring his head to David. David condemns them and orders their execution. The account also recalls Jonathan’s injured son Mephibosheth. Physical disability does not remove his later place in the story.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: distinguish public justice from seeking a reward through another person’s death.

passages.title: David becomes king of Israel and takes Jerusalem
passages.summary: The tribes anoint David at Hebron. He captures Jerusalem, receives help from Hiram, and fights the Philistines. Jerusalem becomes the political center. The capture account contains difficult language about a watercourse and disability. No exact entry route is established here.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies seeking divine guidance.

passages.title: The ark reaches Jerusalem
passages.summary: Uzzah dies during the ark’s transport. The ark stays with Obed Edom before David brings it to Jerusalem. Michal challenges David’s public conduct. Celebration, fear, sacred danger, and household conflict occur together. The narrative does not explain every person’s motives.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the ark’s handling with sacred responsibility. Its proposed motives are interpretations.

passages.title: Nathan announces a promised house
passages.summary: David proposes a house for God. Nathan announces that God will establish David’s house and that his offspring will build a house. House means both a building and a continuing royal family. Scholarly discussion distinguishes the dynastic promise from later messianic interpretation.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the promised house with Jesus Christ.

passages.title: Wars, tribute, and royal officials
passages.summary: The chapter collects David’s campaigns, tribute, dedicated wealth, and court officials. Joab, Zadok, and Benaiah hold named offices. The victories include killing captives and taking wealth. Royal success does not make every action a moral example.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: include defeated people when assessing descriptions of a powerful kingdom.

passages.title: Mephibosheth receives land and a place at the table
passages.summary: David seeks a surviving member of Saul’s household for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba identifies Mephibosheth, whom David brings from Machir’s house. A former rival’s descendant receives provision. His disability remains part of his description, not evidence of lesser worth.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies David’s kindness to Jonathan’s son.

passages.title: Humiliated envoys and war with Ammon
passages.summary: Hanun humiliates David’s messengers. Ammon hires allies. Joab and Abishai divide their forces, and the conflict expands. Suspicion turns an intended condolence into public humiliation and war. The guide does not reconstruct all battle positions.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: assess information before assuming hostile intent.

passages.title: David takes Bathsheba and arranges Uriah’s death
passages.summary: David sends for Bathsheba while Uriah serves at Rabbah. After she reports pregnancy, David arranges Uriah’s death through Joab. The king controls access, orders, and the cover-up. The account condemns David. It does not report Bathsheba’s consent or make her responsible for his commands.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies resisting temptation and David’s harmful choices. This application does not transfer responsibility to Bathsheba.

passages.title: Nathan confronts David and the child dies
passages.summary: Nathan uses a story to confront David. David confesses. The unnamed infant dies, Solomon is later born, and Rabbah is taken. The child’s death raises a difficult question about suffering after another person’s wrongdoing. The guide does not make a sick child morally responsible.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual cites a Joseph Smith Translation reading that differs from the reading text at 12:13.

passages.title: Amnon assaults Tamar and Absalom takes revenge
passages.summary: Jonadab advises Amnon’s deception. Amnon rapes Tamar and expels her. Absalom later orders Amnon’s killing and flees. Tamar clearly protests and publicly expresses grief. Responsibility belongs to the attacker. Revenge does not restore her safety or tell readers her later life.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: hear Tamar’s words and consider the failure to protect her.

passages.title: The woman of Tekoa and Absalom’s return
passages.summary: Joab sends a wise woman to persuade David through a constructed legal appeal. Absalom returns, then later regains access to David. A persuasive story can expose inconsistent judgment but also serve a political plan. Returning to the city does not immediately restore the relationship.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: test a persuasive argument without ignoring the person who arranged it.

passages.title: Absalom gathers support and David leaves Jerusalem
passages.summary: Absalom promises better justice and begins a revolt from Hebron. David leaves Jerusalem. Ittai stays with him, while Hushai returns as his agent. Claims about justice gain political force. The flight also depends on foreigners, priests, messengers, and household members.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: compare promises of justice with the methods used to gain power.

passages.title: Ziba’s accusation, Shimei’s curses, and Absalom’s public act
passages.summary: Ziba accuses Mephibosheth. Shimei curses David. Hushai approaches Absalom, who follows Ahithophel’s advice concerning David’s concubines. The reader later hears Mephibosheth’s conflicting account. The concubines become targets in a public struggle over kingship.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: do not treat an accusation as proof before hearing the affected person.

passages.title: Hushai’s counsel and the messengers’ escape
passages.summary: Absalom rejects Ahithophel’s immediate attack plan for Hushai’s advice. Two women help messages reach David. Allies bring supplies at Mahanaim. The escape depends on people outside the royal council. Food, shelter, and risk matter alongside strategy. Ahithophel’s death remains a tragic part of the account.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: identify the care and practical help that make survival possible.

passages.title: Absalom dies and David grieves
passages.summary: David orders his commanders to deal gently with Absalom. Joab kills Absalom, and a Cushite messenger reports the outcome. David mourns his son. Victory for the king and devastating personal loss occur together. The text says Absalom’s head catches in the tree, not specifically his hair.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: allow grief without reducing a family member to political allegiance.

passages.title: David returns and hears competing claims
passages.summary: Joab confronts David’s withdrawal. David returns, spares Shimei, hears Mephibosheth, and offers care to Barzillai, who sends Chimham instead. Mephibosheth disputes Ziba’s account. David divides the land without the narrative resolving every factual question. Tribal rivalry remains.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: distinguish restored authority from fully repaired relationships.

passages.title: Sheba’s revolt and the wise woman of Abel
passages.summary: Sheba leads another revolt. Joab kills Amasa. A wise woman negotiates during the siege of Abel, and the townspeople kill Sheba. The woman challenges the destruction of a whole town. Her intervention saves the city, while its resolution still includes a violent death.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual states that David’s concubines were not responsible for Absalom’s violation.

passages.title: Rizpah guards the dead and warriors defend David
passages.summary: David hands seven descendants of Saul to the Gibeonites. Rizpah guards their exposed bodies. Later scenes recall battles with Philistine warriors. Two Mephibosheths are distinct here. The executed sons must remain visible. The Hebrew Goliath reading differs from this translation’s harmonized wording.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual questions the executions under the law against punishing children for parents’ sins.

passages.title: David’s song of deliverance
passages.summary: David praises God through images of rescue, storm, battle, and protection. The song closely parallels Psalm 18. Poetry expresses remembered deliverance and claimed integrity. Readers should also retain the prose account’s criticism of David’s conduct.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: compare a person’s self-description with actions elsewhere in the narrative.

passages.title: Last words and remembered warriors
passages.summary: David’s final oracle describes righteous rule. The chapter lists warriors and recalls risky service, including the water from Bethlehem. The account collects memory rather than providing a continuous event sequence. Uriah’s inclusion keeps the victim of David’s command within the list.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: compare righteous rule in the poem with the king’s responsibilities toward those who serve him.

passages.title: The census, plague, and Araunah’s threshing floor
passages.summary: David orders a census despite Joab’s objection. Gad announces judgment. David buys Araunah’s threshing floor and offers sacrifice after the plague. David asks why the people suffer for his wrongdoing. Samuel attributes the incitement to God, while 1 Chronicles 21 attributes it to Satan.
passages.uncertainty: Named localities and broad settings only. Exact houses, battle positions, and travel paths remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual notes the different account in Chronicles. Its proposed census motive remains an interpretation.

events.detail: Poetry expresses remembered deliverance and claimed integrity. Readers should also retain the prose account’s criticism of David’s conduct.

events.title: Last words and remembered warriors
events.summary: David’s final oracle describes righteous rule. The chapter lists warriors and recalls risky service, including the water from Bethlehem.
events.detail: The account collects memory rather than providing a continuous event sequence. Uriah’s inclusion keeps the victim of David’s command within the list.

events.title: The census, plague, and Araunah’s threshing floor
events.summary: David orders a census despite Joab’s objection. Gad announces judgment. David buys Araunah’s threshing floor and offers sacrifice after the plague.
events.detail: David asks why the people suffer for his wrongdoing. Samuel attributes the incitement to God, while 1 Chronicles 21 attributes it to Satan.

guides.title: Study 2 Samuel
guides.description: Follow selected chapters through the book.

steps.title: David laments Saul and Jonathan
steps.text: An Amalekite brings Saul’s royal objects and claims to have killed him. David orders his death, then laments Saul and Jonathan. The messenger’s claim differs from 1 Samuel 31. The guide preserves that difference instead of treating both accounts as identical.

steps.title: Amnon assaults Tamar and Absalom takes revenge
steps.text: Jonadab advises Amnon’s deception. Amnon rapes Tamar and expels her. Absalom later orders Amnon’s killing and flees. Tamar clearly protests and publicly expresses grief. Responsibility belongs to the attacker. Revenge does not restore her safety or tell readers her later life.

steps.title: The census, plague, and Araunah’s threshing floor
steps.text: David orders a census despite Joab’s objection. Gad announces judgment. David buys Araunah’s threshing floor and offers sacrifice after the plague. David asks why the people suffer for his wrongdoing. Samuel attributes the incitement to God, while 1 Chronicles 21 attributes it to Satan.

textRoutes.title: Two kingdoms and the battle at Gibeon
textRoutes.summary: Judah anoints David at Hebron. Abner installs Ishbosheth at Mahanaim. Fighting at Gibeon leads to Asahel’s death.
textRoutes.detail: A contest expands into broader killing. The division and pursuit reveal the human costs of succession.

textRoutes.title: Abner changes allegiance and Joab kills him
textRoutes.summary: After conflict with Ishbosheth over Rizpah, Abner negotiates with David. Michal is returned. Joab kills Abner, and David mourns.
textRoutes.detail: Women’s household positions enter negotiations over power. David publicly rejects responsibility for Abner’s killing.

textRoutes.title: David becomes king of Israel and takes Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: The tribes anoint David at Hebron. He captures Jerusalem, receives help from Hiram, and fights the Philistines.
textRoutes.detail: Jerusalem becomes the political center. The capture account contains difficult language about a watercourse and disability. No exact entry route is established here.

textRoutes.title: The ark reaches Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: Uzzah dies during the ark’s transport. The ark stays with Obed Edom before David brings it to Jerusalem. Michal challenges David’s public conduct.
textRoutes.detail: Celebration, fear, sacred danger, and household conflict occur together. The narrative does not explain every person’s motives.

textRoutes.title: Amnon assaults Tamar and Absalom takes revenge
textRoutes.summary: Jonadab advises Amnon’s deception. Amnon rapes Tamar and expels her. Absalom later orders Amnon’s killing and flees.
textRoutes.detail: Tamar clearly protests and publicly expresses grief. Responsibility belongs to the attacker. Revenge does not restore her safety or tell readers her later life.

textRoutes.summary: Absalom promises better justice and begins a revolt from Hebron. David leaves Jerusalem. Ittai stays with him, while Hushai returns as his agent.
textRoutes.detail: Claims about justice gain political force. The flight also depends on foreigners, priests, messengers, and household members.

textRoutes.title: Hushai’s counsel and the messengers’ escape
textRoutes.summary: Absalom rejects Ahithophel’s immediate attack plan for Hushai’s advice. Two women help messages reach David. Allies bring supplies at Mahanaim.
textRoutes.detail: The escape depends on people outside the royal council. Food, shelter, and risk matter alongside strategy. Ahithophel’s death remains a tragic part of the account.

textRoutes.title: David returns and hears competing claims
textRoutes.summary: Joab confronts David’s withdrawal. David returns, spares Shimei, hears Mephibosheth, and offers care to Barzillai, who sends Chimham instead.
textRoutes.detail: Mephibosheth disputes Ziba’s account. David divides the land without the narrative resolving every factual question. Tribal rivalry remains.

textRoutes.title: Sheba’s revolt and the wise woman of Abel
textRoutes.summary: Sheba leads another revolt. Joab kills Amasa. A wise woman negotiates during the siege of Abel, and the townspeople kill Sheba.
textRoutes.detail: The woman challenges the destruction of a whole town. Her intervention saves the city, while its resolution still includes a violent death.

textRoutes.title: Rizpah guards the dead and warriors defend David
textRoutes.summary: David hands seven descendants of Saul to the Gibeonites. Rizpah guards their exposed bodies. Later scenes recall battles with Philistine warriors.
textRoutes.detail: Two Mephibosheths are distinct here. The executed sons must remain visible. The Hebrew Goliath reading differs from this translation’s harmonized wording.
